news.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
paras: NASA is planning to send astronauts to the Moon with new plans. The Orion spacecraft was built by Lockheed Martin for other missions. The new plans tell Orion to fly the opposite way, which it was not built to do.

Because of this, liquids inside Orion’s tanks might move wrong, risking problems. Scientists will tweak the tanks so the fuel stays where it should be. If they don’t fix it, the spacecraft could fail on the Moon trip.

news.title: Woman entered hibernation-like state during winter for more than 30 years
paras: A post-mortem analysis suggests this might have been caused by a reduced number of connections between neurons in a brain region called the hypothalamus. Some warm-blooded animals – such as dormice and ground squirrels – can enter a state called torpor, in which they become less active, reduce their body temperature and slow their metabolism to save energy.

Prolonged torpor, known as hibernation, usually occurs during the winter, when food is scarce and temperatures drop. While humans don’t have this ability, some researchers think we may have the genetic hardware to enter a reduced energy state, and discovering how to trigger this could have health benefits.

news.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
paras: a fighting chance Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things Watching fights wasn’t as good as practical experience, but it got the mice halfway there. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout.

Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day.

And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe.

news.title: Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)
paras: From colorful meteors to lingering trails, the Leonids put on a great show this year. The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot.

And for some, their patience certainly paid off. Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

news.title: This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researcher
paras: Add as preferred source Jeremy Bentham's mummified head undergoes a CT scan. Tannis Davidson As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration. And he made good on his promise.

Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights. UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head. They share the process and their findings in a short film called Bentham Revealed .

news.title: The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Enda
paras: Add as preferred source North Atlantic right whales can weigh up to 140,000 pounds. New England Aquarium The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.

Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales. Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
